summary: Both target files are stubs: `verify()` is `return false;` and `handle()` returns `WP_REST_Response(['ok'=>false], 401)`. Nothing in the WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md pipeline is implemented yet, so this is a greenfield answer rather than a bug review. I could not find a WP core checkout on this machine (D:\dev\_apollo.rio.br holds only wp-content; the LocalWP sites at C:\Users\User\Local Sites\{a,fim} contain only wp-content too), so every assertion below is verified against WordPress/wordpress-develop trunk source fetched directly, with the exact function bodies quoted as evidence. Headline results: (1) use `WP_REST_Request::get_body()`, not `php://input` — WP has already consumed the stream via `WP_REST_Server::get_raw_data()` before `permission_callback` runs; (2) a bare `return false` yields 403, not 401, whenever the caller is authenticated (Application Passwords is the realistic path) — the spec's "always 401" requires an explicit `WP_Error(..., array('status'=>401))`; (3) `get_header('x-webhook-hmac')` is correct but returns `null`, which is a PHP 8 TypeError in `hash_equals`; (4) transients have no atomic add — `add_option()` is an `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` upsert, so two simultaneous POSTs both pass dedupe; (5) `wp_get_environment_type()` returns `'production'` on LocalWP by default, which combined with `is_ssl()` being false behind any TLS-terminating proxy is the single most likely cause of a permanently-401 webhook; (6) the highest-severity fail-OPEN trap is `status_header()`'s `if ( ! headers_sent() ) ` guard — one PHP notice printed during dispatch makes every auth failure return HTTP 200.

findings.topic: 1. RAW BODY — use WP_REST_Request::get_body(); php://input is already consumed
findings.answer: Use `$request->get_body()`. It is the authoritative raw byte string and it is what WP itself will later parse into JSON params, so signing it guarantees verify-parse consistency. YES, WP has already consumed php://input before your permission_callback runs: `WP_REST_Server::serve_request()` calls `$request->set_body( self::get_raw_data() )` UNCONDITIONALLY, and `get_raw_data()` does `file_get_contents('php://input')`. Re-readability: on PHP >= 5.6 (WP 6.x requires 7.2+) php://input is buffered by the SAPI and re-readable, so a second read normally works — but there are three configurations where it does not. (a) `enctype=multipart/form-data` POST with `enable_post_data_reading=On` (the default): PHP docs state php://input 'is not available' — it returns an empty string, for WP and for you alike. (b) `enable_post_data_reading=Off`: PHP does not buffer, the stream is one-shot forward-only, WP reads it first and you get ''. (c) CLI/WP-CLI SAPI: php://input is STDIN. There is a fourth, subtler case that makes php://input outright WRONG rather than merely fragile: internal dispatch. `rest_do_request()` calls `rest_get_server()->dispatch( $request )` directly — no serve_request, no php://input involvement. If any plugin or `rest_preload_api_request` dispatches your route internally, `file_get_contents('php://input')` returns the OUTER HTTP request's body, not this WP_REST_Request's body. HMACing that and then handling `$request->get_json_params()` is a genuine signature/payload mismatch. Also note `get_raw_data()` caches into the `$HTTP_RAW_POST_DATA` global, so calling it repeatedly never re-touches the stream. Safe fallback order: get_body() -> WP_REST_Server::get_raw_data() -> file_get_contents('php://input'), and an empty result must be a hard 401, never a 'skip verification' branch.

findings.topic: 2. STATUS CODES — bare `false` gives 403 for authenticated callers; force 401 with WP_Error status
findings.answer: A bare `return false` (and `return null`, and a callback with no return statement) produces `new WP_Error('rest_forbidden', 'Sorry, you are not allowed to do that.', array('status' => rest_authorization_required_code()))`. `rest_authorization_required_code()` is literally `return is_user_logged_in() ? 403 : 401;`. So the emitted status is caller-dependent: 401 anonymous, 403 authenticated. That is a spec violation for an endpoint whose contract is 'every auth failure is 401'. The logged-in case is NOT hypothetical. `rest_cookie_check_errors()` (hooked at priority 100 on rest_authentication_errors) zeroes the user only on the cookie path: if no nonce is present it calls `wp_set_current_user(0)` and returns true, so a cookie-only caller lands at 401. But its FIRST guard is `if ( true !== $wp_rest_auth_cookie && is_user_logged_in() ) { return $result; }` — a caller authenticated by any non-cookie mechanism keeps its identity. Core ships exactly such a mechanism: `add_filter( 'determine_current_user', 'wp_validate_application_password', 20 )`. Any Application Password (or a JWT/Basic-Auth plugin) makes `is_user_logged_in()` true, and your bare `false` becomes 403. A cookie-authed browser sending a valid `X-WP-Nonce` also stays logged in -> 403. CONFIRMED: a WP_Error returned from permission_callback propagates verbatim. `respond_to_request()` does `if ( is_wp_error( $permission ) ) { $response = $permission; }` with no rewriting; `rest_ensure_response()` returns WP_Error untouched; `error_to_response()` -> `rest_convert_error_to_response()` extracts the status; `serve_request()` does `$code = $result->get_status(); $this->set_status( $code );` -> `status_header( $code )`. 401 maps to 'Unauthorized' and 413 to 'Request Entity Too Large' in `get_status_header_desc()`, so both are emitted correctly. TWO TRAPS inside `rest_convert_error_to_response()`: (a) the default status is 500 — `new WP_Error('code','msg')` with NO data array yields HTTP 500, not 401; (b) it `array_reduce`s over `get_all_error_data()` and the LAST numeric status wins, so `$err->add('other','msg', array('status'=>500))` silently overrides your 401. Use one code, one data array. 413 behaves identically — same mechanism, same requirement to pass `array('status'=>413)`.

findings.topic: 3. HEADERS — get_header() canonicalisation, null return, duplicates, underscore collision
findings.answer: `WP_REST_Request::canonicalize_header_name()` is `strtolower()` then `str_replace('-','_')`. So dashes and underscores are equivalent and lookup is fully case-insensitive. `get_header('x-webhook-hmac')` IS correct for an incoming `X-Webhook-Hmac`, and so are `'X-Webhook-Hmac'`, `'x_webhook_hmac'` and `'X_WEBHOOK_HMAC'` — all four resolve to the same internal key. The chain is: `X-Webhook-Hmac` -> `$_SERVER['HTTP_X_WEBHOOK_HMAC']` -> `WP_REST_Server::get_headers()` strips the `HTTP_` prefix -> key `X_WEBHOOK_HMAC` -> `set_header()` canonicalises -> `x_webhook_hmac`. Three concrete gotchas. (a) ABSENT HEADER RETURNS `null`, not `''` or `false`. `hash_equals( $calc, null )` is a TypeError on PHP 8 -> uncaught fatal -> HTTP 500, not your 401. Always cast: `(string) $request->get_header(...)`. (b) DUPLICATES: `get_header()` does `implode( ',', $this->headers[$key] )`. Headers from `$_SERVER` arrive as one string (Apache pre-joins repeats with ', '), so a duplicated signature header yields a value that simply fails `hash_equals` — fail-closed, which is fine, but use `get_header_as_array()` if you want to reject duplication explicitly rather than silently. (c) UNDERSCORE COLLISION: `X_Webhook_Hmac` and `X-Webhook-Hmac` both become `$_SERVER['HTTP_X_WEBHOOK_HMAC']`. nginx drops underscore headers by default (`underscores_in_headers off`), Apache passes them; if a front proxy sanitises the dashed form but not the underscored one, PHP can end up seeing the attacker's value. SPOOFING: every `X-*` header here is fully attacker-controlled by design — only the HMAC over the body proves origin, so never make a trust decision from `X-Webhook-*` alone, and never trust `X-Forwarded-For` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` for authorisation. One more reason to prefer `get_header()` over raw `$_SERVER`: `wp_magic_quotes()` runs `$_SERVER = add_magic_quotes( $_SERVER )` at boot, so reading `$_SERVER['HTTP_X_WEBHOOK_HMAC']` directly gives you a SLASHED value; `serve_request()` undoes this with `wp_unslash( $_SERVER )` before building the request. (Harmless for hex, wrong in general.) Finally, `Authorization` is special-cased via `REDIRECT_HTTP_AUTHORIZATION` — irrelevant today but relevant if you ever move to a bearer token.

findings.topic: 4. TRANSIENTS — not autoloaded when expiring, false for both expired and absent, and NO atomic add
findings.answer: NO PERSISTENT OBJECT CACHE (the LocalWP default and most shared hosts): the value lives in `wp_options`. Crucially, a transient WITH an expiration is stored with autoload = false — `add_option( $transient_option, $value, '', false )` — so it is NOT in alloptions and does NOT bloat the autoload payload. Each `get_transient()` therefore costs a `wp_prime_option_caches()` DB round trip (it primes both the value and the `_transient_timeout_` row in one query). EXPIRED vs ABSENT: indistinguishable — both return exactly `false`. On read, if `$timeout < time()` core deletes BOTH options and sets `$value = false`; an absent key falls through to `get_option()` which also returns `false`. There is no third state, so you can never store a literal `false` as a dedupe marker (store `1` or a timestamp). Expired rows are only reaped lazily on read or by the daily `delete_expired_transients()` cron, so a high-volume webhook with a 10-minute TTL leaves rows accumulating between cron runs. RACE: YES, absolutely. `get_transient()` then `set_transient()` is a textbook TOCTOU. Two simultaneous identical POSTs both see `false`, both process, both write. Worse, `set_transient()` cannot save you, because `add_option()` is NOT an atomic insert — its SQL is `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, a plain upsert, and its only 'does it exist' check is a read-then-write `get_option()` comparison at the top. ATOMIC PRIMITIVES IN WP: there is no atomic add in the transient or option API. Two real options. (a) `wp_cache_add()` — atomic ONLY when a persistent backend implements it atomically (Memcached ADD, Redis SETNX). With the default in-process `WP_Object_Cache` it is per-request and useless across requests, so it is not a portable answer. (b) The canonical core pattern, `WP_Upgrader::create_lock()`: `INSERT IGNORE` into wp_options and test the affected-row count. That IS atomic (option_name carries a UNIQUE index). Do not mix that raw SQL with get_transient/set_transient, because under a persistent object cache the transient API reads wp_cache_get and would never see your row. KEY LENGTH: 172 characters max, documented in core ('Must be 172 characters or fewer in length'). The arithmetic: option_name is VARCHAR(191) and the longest prefix is `_transient_timeout_` at 19 chars. This matters directly here — `X-Webhook-Request-Id` is attacker-controlled and arbitrarily long. Overflow means silent truncation in non-strict MySQL (-> collisions, i.e. a forged replay looking like a dupe) or a failed query in strict mode. Hash it.

findings.topic: 5. do_action from a REST handler — runs before the response, but it BLOCKS it
findings.answer: YES, guaranteed. The whole REST stack runs synchronously inside one PHP request: `add_action( 'parse_request', 'rest_api_loaded' )` -> `rest_api_loaded()` -> `$server->serve_request( $route )` -> `check_authentication()` -> `dispatch()` -> your callback -> your `do_action()` listeners -> `rest_post_dispatch` filter -> `send_headers()` -> `$code = $result->get_status(); $this->set_status( $code );` -> `echo $result`. Your listeners complete before a single byte of the JSON body is emitted and before the status header is set. Five caveats worth planning around. (a) IT BLOCKS THE RESPONSE. WP does not call `fastcgi_finish_request()`. A listener that does `wp_remote_post()` back to WAHA holds the webhook connection open; if WAHA's client timeout fires it retries, and you get duplicate deliveries. Always write the dedupe marker BEFORE dispatching slow work. (b) IF A LISTENER ECHOES ANYTHING (a stray `var_dump`, a PHP notice with display_errors on) `headers_sent()` becomes true and the later `status_header()` call silently no-ops — see topic 7. (c) AN UNCAUGHT THROWABLE in a listener is a fatal, i.e. 500, and WAHA will retry. Wrap listener-dispatched work if you want a clean 200. (d) HOOK REGISTRATION WINDOW: `parse_request` fires after `init` and `wp_loaded`, so anything registered on `init` is present — but hooks registered on `template_redirect`, `wp`, or `wp_footer` never fire on a REST request at all, because `rest_api_loaded()` ends the request right after `serve_request()`. `shutdown` still runs (WP registers `shutdown_action_hook` via `register_shutdown_function`), so `shutdown` listeners execute after the body is flushed — that is the closest thing to fire-and-forget available without fastcgi_finish_request. (e) DEFERRING TO CRON DOES NOT DEFER AT ALL IN THIS REQUEST: `wp_cron()` is hooked to `init`, which already ran before `parse_request`, so a `wp_schedule_single_event( time(), ... )` created in your handler is not spawned by this request — it waits for the next front-end hit. Do not treat it as 'runs in a second'.

findings.topic: 6. is_ssl() behind a proxy, and wp_get_environment_type() on LocalWP
findings.answer: `is_ssl()` inspects ONLY `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` ('on' or '1') and `$_SERVER['SERVER_PORT'] === '443'`. It knows nothing about `X-Forwarded-Proto`. When a load balancer, Cloudflare, nginx reverse proxy, or a Docker ingress terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to PHP on port 80, `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` is unset and SERVER_PORT is 80 — `is_ssl()` returns false on a site that is genuinely HTTPS end-to-end. A rule like `if ( ! is_ssl() ) return 401;` locks out exactly the production deployment it was meant to protect, permanently and silently. (Note this repo already ships `really-simple-ssl` in wp-content/plugins, whose whole job is patching `$_SERVER['HTTPS']='on'` from the forwarded header — if it is deactivated or load-ordered after your check, is_ssl() flips.) LOCALWP: `wp_get_environment_type()` returns 'production'. LocalWP does not define `WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE` in the generated wp-config.php and does not set the env var, and core's final guard is `if ( ! in_array( $current_env, $wp_environments, true ) ) { $current_env = 'production'; }`. So the combination 'production environment' + 'is_ssl() false' is the DEFAULT state of a LocalWP site — which means a naive `if ( 'production' === wp_get_environment_type() && ! is_ssl() ) deny;` is an always-401 webhook in the lab, which is precisely the scenario the SSOT's 'LocalWP lab allowed' line is trying to avoid. Also note the static cache: `static $current_env` short-circuits after the first call, so defining `WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE` from a plugin file is too late — it must be in wp-config.php. RECOMMENDED CHECK: gate on the site's own CONFIGURED scheme (`home_url()`), which is site configuration rather than request data and therefore not spoofable, and treat request-level signals as an OR-widening, never as the sole gate. `X-Forwarded-Proto` is client-supplied and trivially forged when the app is directly reachable, so use it only to widen acceptance, never to deny.

findings.topic: 7a. FAIL-OPEN TRAP — permission_callback only denies on strict `false` or `null`
findings.answer: The deny branch is `elseif ( false === $permission || null === $permission )` — strict identity. Every other return value is treated as ALLOWED. `return 0;`, `return '';`, `return '0';`, `return array();`, `return new WP_REST_Response(...)` — all pass the gate and the handler executes. This is the classic silent always-accept: a helper that returns `0` on failure, or a refactor that changes `return false` to `return $count_of_valid_signatures`, opens the door with no error anywhere. Related and equally fatal: the check is guarded by `! empty( $handler['permission_callback'] )`. If the key is ever removed, misspelled, or set to an empty value, NO permission check runs at all and the route is fully public. Since WP 5.5 `register_rest_route()` emits a `_doing_it_wrong()` notice when permission_callback is missing, but it STILL REGISTERS AND SERVES THE ROUTE — the notice is not a guard. Finally, core does not wrap `call_user_func( $handler['permission_callback'], $request )` in try/catch, so an uncaught Throwable inside `verify()` becomes a fatal 500 rather than your 401 — and if `WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY` is on, the fatal text is echoed, which also trips trap 7b.

findings.topic: 7b. FAIL-OPEN TRAP — one stray byte of output makes every response HTTP 200
findings.answer: `status_header()` ends with `if ( ! headers_sent() ) { header( $status_header, true, $code ); }`. `WP_REST_Server::set_status()` is nothing but `status_header( $code )`, and it is called AFTER dispatch. So if anything has already produced output by then — a PHP notice or deprecation with display_errors on, a `var_dump`, whitespace or a BOM after `?>` in any loaded plugin file, a debug `echo` in a `do_action` listener, an `E_WARNING` from a mistyped array index — PHP flushes the buffered 200 headers on that first byte, `headers_sent()` becomes true, and the 401/413 is silently dropped. The client receives HTTP 200 with the error text prepended to the JSON. An HMAC webhook that answers 200 to every forged request looks perfectly healthy in logs. There is a second, quieter form of the same bug: `status_header()` returns early without sending anything when the description is empty (`if ( empty( $description ) ) { return; }`), and `get_status_header_desc()` returns `''` for any code not in its table. 401 and 413 are both in the table so they are safe, but a custom code (say 499, or any invented value) silently leaves the response at 200. This environment is unusually exposed: LocalWP ships with display_errors on, and there are two active debug logs sitting in wp-content/plugins (debug-161c5c.log, debug-e031aa.log) indicating WP_DEBUG output is being produced.

findings.topic: 7c. FAIL-OPEN TRAP — an unset HMAC key still produces a valid signature
findings.answer: `get_option('apollo_wa_hmac_key')` returns `false` when the option has never been written (activation not run, option deleted, wrong blog on multisite, a failed migration). `hash_hmac('sha512', $raw, false)` does not error — `false` coerces to `''`, and HMAC with an empty key is a perfectly well-defined, computable value. So a plugin whose key option is missing will happily accept any request from anyone who computes `hash_hmac('sha512', $body, '')`. This is not a theoretical bypass: 'the secret is empty' is the first thing an attacker tries against a WordPress HMAC endpoint. On PHP 8.1+ passing `null` (e.g. from `get_option(..., null)`) additionally raises a deprecation, which under display_errors trips trap 7b as well. The fix is a hard length floor before any comparison, not a truthiness check — `if ( ! $key )` catches `false` and `''` but not a 4-character leftover. The SSOT already specifies `wp_generate_password(48, true, true)`, so a >= 32 byte floor is free.
findings.evidence:
PHP semantics, not a WP bug: hash_hmac() accepts an empty key and returns a valid digest. get_option() returns (bool) false for a missing option (src/wp-includes/option.php), and the SSOT stores apollo_wa_hmac_key with autoload=false, so it is absent from alloptions and a missing row is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty value at the call site.

Same class of bug applies to the timestamp window - see the current_time() note in 7d.

findings.topic: 7d. Remaining WP/deployment traps that produce a permanently-401 webhook
findings.answer: Six more, all of which look like 'HMAC is broken' but are not. (1) current_time() TIMEZONE BUG — `current_time('timestamp')` returns site-local time, i.e. UTC plus the GMT offset. This site is Brazilian (apollo.rio.br, America/Sao_Paulo, -03:00), so using it against WAHA's `X-Webhook-Timestamp` skews the comparison by 10,800 seconds and every request fails the +/-5 minute window forever. Use `time()` (always UTC) or `microtime(true)`. Same class of error: WAHA sends UNIX MILLISECONDS while `time()` is seconds — mixing units is a ~1000x skew and a permanent 401. (2) rest_authentication_errors SHORT-CIRCUIT — `check_authentication()` runs BEFORE `dispatch()`, so any plugin returning a WP_Error there kills the request before `verify()` is ever called. Core itself does this via `rest_cookie_check_errors` (`rest_cookie_invalid_nonce`, status 403) for a cookie-bearing request with a bad nonce, and `rest_application_password_check_errors` at priority 90. Security plugins do it too — this install has loginizer-security and really-simple-ssl active. Diagnose by reading the `code` field of the JSON error body: if it is not your `apollo_wa_unauthorized`, your callback never ran. (3) rest_pre_dispatch — a non-null return from that filter short-circuits dispatch entirely, same symptom. (4) PERMALINKS — `/wp-json/...` only exists with pretty permalinks on. The SSOT configures WAHA with `https://apollo.rio.br/wp-json/apollo/v1/wa/webhook`; with plain permalinks that 404s and the fallback is `/?rest_route=/apollo/v1/wa/webhook`. (5) BOOT ORDER — `register_route()` is correctly hooked to `rest_api_init`, but `Apollo_Waha_Plugin::boot()` must run no later than `plugins_loaded`/`init`; anything after `parse_request` means the route is never registered and every call 404s. (6) BODY MUTATION IN TRANSIT — an HTTP 301/302 from http to https (really-simple-ssl's redirect) turns a POST into a GET or drops the body; and if WAHA sends a `Content-Encoding: gzip` body that nginx or a WAF decompresses, WP hashes decompressed bytes while WAHA signed compressed ones — a permanent, perfectly deterministic 401. Point WAHA at the final https URL and confirm no intermediary rewrites the body.
